strengths: Novel and practical combination of moderation classifiers (for coarse screening) with data-attribution (gradient similarity) for fine-grained unsafe training data detection, addressing the real limitation that classifiers are tied to fixed taxonomies and lack insight into training dynamics.

Careful diagnostic analysis (Appendix B.1, Table 8, Figure 1) demonstrating why naively attributing full model responses is noisy due to dilution by benign tokens, which motivates and justifies the design of using externally-identified unsafe subsets as attribution targets for long-form outputs.

Evaluation spans two qualitatively different unsafe-data scenarios (jailbreaking injection and gender-bias injection), showing the method generalizes beyond a single moderation taxonomy, including to a bias setting where standard moderation classifiers are inapplicable.

Goes beyond detection metrics (AUPRC/F1) to show downstream impact: retraining on DABUF-filtered data reduces Attack Success Rate and TPR Gender Gap more than baselines, which is a stronger and more decision-relevant form of evidence than detection accuracy alone.
Ablation on validation-set size (Figure 2) and token-level contribution analysis add useful mechanistic insight into when/why the method works, aiding reproducibility and understanding.
weaknesses: Evaluation sets are very small (Dunsafe of 65-97 samples, Dtest of only 20-30 samples per dataset for ASR), and most main results (Tables 1-4, 6-7) appear to be single-run numbers without confidence intervals or repeated trials, raising concerns about the statistical reliability of reported differences, especially for ASR percentages computed over 20-30 test prompts.

The method still depends on a moderation classifier (Llama-Guard-3-8B) plus manual human annotation to build the target set for long-form/jailbreaking scenarios, which partially undercuts the paper's central claim of removing dependence on predefined taxonomies and additional curation effort; the human-annotation step is not quantified in terms of cost/effort/inter-annotator agreement.

No baseline or discussion of DABUF's computational cost (gradient computation across the ~40k-sample training set, per target) relative to the classifiers it is compared against, despite the paper motivating DABUF partly by classifiers' "significant computational overhead"; related work explicitly notes attribution methods are themselves computationally intensive, making this omission notable.

Gender bias experiments use a synthetic, fully-controlled label-corruption injection (physician→nurse) rather than naturally occurring bias, and only compares against a single weak baseline (Ada3 embeddings) with no comparison to other influence-based or bias-specific detection methods, limiting the strength of generalization claims in that setting.

On XSTest-Response, Wildguard (an existing classifier) outperforms DABUF in AUPRC and F1, which is explained post-hoc as being due to in-distribution alignment with Wildguard's training data; this weakens the paper's headline claim of consistently "outperforming SOTA" and suggests the advantage of DABUF may be scenario-dependent rather than general.

The improvement percentages quoted in the abstract (7.5%, 44.1%) appear to be absolute percentage-point differences rather than relative improvements, which could be presented more precisely/clearly to avoid overstating impact.

The experimental setup (very low injection ratios <0.025%, LoRA-based gradient computation, single model families) is somewhat narrow, and it remains unclear how well the approach scales to larger, more heterogeneous real-world training corpora or full-parameter fine-tuning, a limitation acknowledged only partially in the Limitations section.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: moderation-classifier-based unsafe data detection is taxonomy-bound and does not account for a data point's actual causal influence on model outputs during training, which is a legitimate gap.

The token-level noise analysis in Appendix B.1 (per-token AUPRC, effect of number of top-contributing tokens) provides a reasonable diagnostic motivating why naive full-sequence attribution fails on long-form outputs.
Demonstrating the approach on two qualitatively different tasks (jailbreak injection detection and gender-bias data detection) is a nice attempt to show flexibility beyond a single narrow taxonomy.
The overall pipeline (attribution + optional classifier-assisted target refinement + retraining evaluation) is conceptually simple and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central claim that DABUF avoids the overhead/rigidity of moderation classifiers is undermined by its own design: in the jailbreak setting (the paper's flagship results), DABUF explicitly relies on Llama-Guard-3-8B to produce a candidate set plus manual human annotation to build Didentified. This is not a fair apples-to-apples comparison with zero-shot baseline classifiers, since DABUF is given extra human-verified supervision that the baselines do not receive; the AUPRC/F1 gains could simply reflect this additional labeled information rather than a superior attribution mechanism.

Reported gains are inconsistent and partly cherry-picked: DABUF is clearly outperformed by Wildguard on XSTest-Response (AUPRC 74.1 vs 85.9; F1 68.7 vs 71.1), yet the abstract advertises only the favorable ToxicChat number ('up to 7.5%'), giving a misleading impression of consistent superiority.

Experimental scale is very small: unsafe-injection counts are tiny (Dunsafe = 97, 65, 150 examples), test sets for ASR evaluation contain only 20–30 prompts, and injection ratios are below 0.025%. Nearly all main-result tables (Tables 1–7) report single-run numbers with no variance/confidence intervals, so the statistical reliability of the reported differences (e.g., 5% vs 15% vs 25% ASR on a 20-sample test set) is highly questionable.

The method's practical flexibility claim is weakened by its own limitation section: for long-form/noisy outputs it still requires externally identified unsafe examples similar in nature to the target unsafe behavior, meaning it cannot bootstrap detection of a genuinely novel unsafe category without already having labeled instances of it — arguably no more taxonomy-free than existing classifiers.

No comparison against other established data-attribution techniques (e.g., DataInf, LESS/gradient-based alternatives cited in related work) is provided; only Pruthi et al.'s gradient-similarity method is used, and it is not shown that the reported improvements are due to the 'data attribution' framing per se versus this specific choice of attribution estimator.

No analysis of computational cost is given despite the abstract explicitly criticizing baseline classifiers for 'significant computational overhead' — gradient-based attribution over an LLM's parameters (even after LoRA/random projection) is itself known to be costly, and this trade-off is never quantified or compared against baseline inference costs.

Filtering evaluation is limited to an arbitrary top-K=100 threshold with no exploration of how K should be chosen in practice, nor of the precision/recall trade-offs at different removal budgets, limiting practical applicability.

The gender-bias experiment uses a single dataset (Bias in Bios) with a single, narrowly engineered corruption pattern (female physician→nurse), and the only baseline is a generic embedding similarity method (Ada3); this is a weak comparison set that does not establish generalizability of the approach to other bias types or more competitive detection baselines.

The paper's presentation contains some looseness (e.g., 'we first an LLM-based classifier' missing a verb; inconsistent capitalization of dataset splits), and important experimental details (e.g., variance across repeated retraining runs, sensitivity to random seed in LoRA fine-tuning) are largely absent from the main text.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem—identifying and removing unsafe training data—with a novel angle: using data attribution rather than trained moderation classifiers, which in principle removes dependence on predefined safety taxonomies.

The key technical insight in Section 3 and Appendix B.1 (that naive whole-sequence gradient attribution is diluted by benign tokens, and that unsafe tokens carry disproportionately larger gradients) is a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution, supported by token-level precision analysis (Table 8) and the top-N token filtering experiment (Figure 1).

The proposed fix—using a small, human-verified subset of externally identified unsafe examples as the attribution target for long-form outputs—is a sensible and practical design choice that is empirically validated (Table 9/10 show large gains over naive response-based attribution).

Evaluation spans two qualitatively different unsafe-data scenarios (jailbreaking injection and gender bias), which helps demonstrate the claimed flexibility/taxonomy-independence of the approach; the paper reports downstream retraining results (ASR, TPR Gender Gap) in addition to detection metrics, giving an end-to-end validation of practical usefulness rather than detection accuracy alone.

Reasonable set of baselines for the jailbreaking setting (OpenAI Moderation, Llama-Guard-3-8B, Wildguard, GradSafe) and an ablation on validation-set size (Appendix B.2) showing the method still beats SOTA classifiers with very few validation examples.

The limitations section is candid, discussing homogeneous injection assumptions, lack of fine-grained taxonomy, and adversarial vulnerability of influence estimation—appropriate self-critique rather than hiding weaknesses.
weaknesses: The central claim of taxonomy-independence is partially undermined in the jailbreaking setting: DABUF still relies on Llama-Guard-3-8B to produce the candidate set Dcand, plus human annotation to obtain Didentified. This makes the comparison against Llama-Guard-3-8B as a baseline somewhat unfair (DABUF is essentially Llama-Guard-3-8B + human curation + attribution), and the paper does not clearly quantify how much of the gain is attributable to attribution vs. to the human-verified candidate set.

Experimental scale is quite small: unsafe injection sets are on the order of 65–150 samples, test sets for ASR evaluation are only 20–30 examples, and only two model backbones (Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B) are used. No variance/confidence intervals are reported for the main detection and retraining tables (only the validation-set-size ablation includes repeated sampling with std), making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements (e.g., 7.5% and 44.1% headline gains).

The method is only compared against moderation-classifier baselines and one gradient-based method (GradSafe); no comparison is made against other data-attribution techniques mentioned in the related work (e.g., DataInf, LESS, Data Shapley variants), leaving it unclear whether gradient-similarity (Pruthi et al.) is the best attribution backbone for this task or just a convenient choice.

Scalability of the attribution-based approach to realistic large-scale training corpora (millions of samples) is not demonstrated; the benign pool used (~40k for jailbreaking, ~10k for bias) is modest, and the paper does not report wall-clock/compute cost of the gradient-similarity computation relative to baseline classifiers, despite computational efficiency being cited in related work as a general concern for attribution methods.

The method assumes unsafe data disproportionately influences unsafe outputs and that a representative Dtarget/Didentified is obtainable; this assumption may not hold for stealthier poisoning/backdoor attacks (acknowledged only briefly in the Limitations/Potential Risks section rather than tested empirically), so robustness under adversarial or low-influence poisoning is unverified.

The gender-bias comparison is thin, with only a single (arguably weak) baseline (Ada3 embedding similarity), so the 44.1% improvement figure is against a baseline not specifically designed for this kind of detection, somewhat inflating the apparent margin of superiority relative to the jailbreaking results where stronger baselines exist.

strengths: The paper provides a principled theoretical grounding for representation-based unsafe data detection via signal detection theory, deriving a discriminability index d' and showing that the optimal linear detector corresponds to a whitened, centered ('Mahalanobis') similarity score, which is an elegant and useful reframing of existing similarity-based attribution methods.

The proposed two-step DRA procedure (whitening + leave-target-out dimension selection) is simple to implement on top of existing methods (GradSim, RepSim) and requires no additional labeled data or classifier training, making it broadly applicable and lightweight compared to moderation classifiers.

Experiments span two distinct and meaningfully different unsafe-data scenarios (jailbreak injection and implicit gender bias) and two model backbones (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it), showing that DRA consistently improves AUPRC over both vanilla attribution baselines and strong moderation classifiers (Llama-Guard, Wildguard), including in the gender-bias setting where classifiers largely fail (e.g., Wildguard AUPRC ~0.06).
Downstream retraining experiments (ASR, TPR Gender Gap) provide evidence that improved detection translates into practically safer models, not just better ranking metrics.

Useful supporting analyses are included: an ablation isolating the contribution of denoising vs. dimension selection (Table 7), t-SNE visualizations showing separability before/after DRA, an empirical check that d' correlates monotonically with AUPRC, and a study of sensitivity to target-set size showing DRA works well even with very few target examples (n=3).
weaknesses: Some retraining/ASR results are modest or inconsistent: e.g., RepSim-DRA yields only marginal ASR reductions in the jailbreak setting (−2.35 and −2.15 percentage points in Table 3), and several DRA-filtered models still retain relatively high ASR (e.g., 43–60%), which weakens the claim that detection gains reliably translate into materially safer retrained models across all configurations.

The key hyperparameter r=30 (number of selected dimensions) and the intermediate candidate-dimension size m' are not justified via sensitivity analysis; it is unclear how robust results are to these choices or how they should be selected in a new setting without ground-truth unsafe labels.

The method's core denoising step requires computing/inverting the covariance matrix Σ_X over the representation space, which for gradient-based representations in LLMs could be very high-dimensional; the paper does not discuss the computational/memory cost of this step or how it scales (LoRA is used to reduce dimensionality, but details and overhead comparisons to baseline classifiers are missing).

The leave-target-out (LTO) surrogate for dimension selection relies on the assumption that the small target set Dtarget is representative of the broader unsafe distribution Dunsafe; while a target-set-size ablation is included, there is limited stress-testing of cases where the target set is biased, narrow, or covers different unsafe genres than the injected data, which is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation.

Evaluation is restricted to a single injection ratio, two specific benign/unsafe dataset pairings per task, and only two mid-sized open-weight model backbones; generalization to larger models, different injection rates, or more heterogeneous/adversarially crafted unsafe data (as noted in the Limitations section) remains untested.

Statistical robustness of results is somewhat limited: ASR is averaged over only 10 inference runs without reported variance/significance, making it hard to assess whether some of the smaller ASR improvements are meaningful versus noise.

The paper does not compare or discuss combining DRA-based attribution with moderation classifiers (a hybrid approach), which could be a natural and practically relevant baseline given that classifiers and attribution methods appear to have complementary strengths (e.g., strong AUPRC for classifiers on jailbreak data vs. attribution's advantage on gender bias).

strengths: The paper grounds the proposed denoising procedure in a principled theoretical framework (signal detection theory, discriminability index d′, and the classical optimal linear detector), which gives a clear rationale for centering, whitening, and dimension selection rather than an ad-hoc heuristic.

The method is evaluated on two qualitatively different unsafe-data scenarios (jailbreak injection and implicit gender bias) and two backbone models, showing that DRA consistently improves both detection AUPRC and downstream safety metrics (ASR, TPR Gender Gap) over vanilla GradSim/RepSim baselines.
Ablation studies (Table 7) isolate the contribution of the whitening/denoising step versus the dimension-selection step, showing both are individually helpful and complementary.
t-SNE visualizations (Appendix C.1) and the d′-vs-AUPRC correlation plot (Appendix D) provide some qualitative and quantitative support for the core denoising hypothesis.
The approach is training-free/label-free relative to moderation classifiers and can, in principle, generalize beyond a fixed taxonomy since it only requires a small target set of unsafe outputs.
weaknesses: No variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing are reported for the main detection (Table 1, 5) or retraining (Table 3, 6) results, despite ASR being described as averaged over 10 runs; several reported gains (e.g., Repsim-DRA ASR 60.0% vs Repsim 63.0% on XSTest, or Repsim-DRA TPR gap changes) are small enough that their reliability cannot be assessed without dispersion statistics.

The filtering protocol's choice of K (number of top-ranked samples removed) appears to rely on knowledge close to the true number of injected unsafe samples (e.g., 'top 500' when only 150 biased samples were injected), which is an oracle-like assumption inconsistent with the stated real-world setting where 'the membership of Dbenign and Dunsafe is unknown'; the paper does not describe how K would be chosen in practice without such knowledge, harming reproducibility and practical applicability.

The construction of the target set Dtarget for the jailbreak experiments (the union of unsafe outputs collected from the very model trained on Dtrain, across the 10 evaluation runs used to compute ASR) raises a potential circularity concern: the target set used to score and filter training data is derived from outputs of a model already trained on that same (still-unfiltered) data, which is not clearly disentangled from the detection evaluation and could inflate benchmarked performance relative to a genuinely blind red-teaming scenario.

Table 1 (detection) and Table 3 (retraining ASR) tell different stories that are not reconciled: RepSim-DRA has by far the highest AUPRC in Table 1, yet GradSim-DRA gives much larger ASR reductions in Table 3; the paper offers only a brief post-hoc explanation ('gradient-based attributions more accurately capture training dynamics') without further analysis, weakening the claim that AUPRC is a reliable surrogate for downstream safety impact, and undercutting the d′-AUPRC monotonicity argument used to motivate the method.

The comparison to moderation-classifier baselines (Llama-Guard, Wildguard, GradSafe) is somewhat apples-to-oranges: these are pre-hoc, model-agnostic classifiers requiring no target set, whereas DRA is inherently post-hoc and needs access to a target set of actual unsafe model outputs; this fundamental difference in assumptions/requirements is acknowledged only briefly and not adequately factored into the comparison or discussion of practical deployability.

The core theoretical contribution (Lemma 3.1, the optimal linear discriminant under known covariance) is a direct application of a classical, well-known result in signal detection/Fisher discriminant analysis rather than a novel theoretical finding, so the 'theoretical grounding' framing somewhat overstates the technical novelty; the real contribution is the practical plug-in estimator and leave-target-out dimension search.

No description or computational-cost analysis is given for how the discrete subset-selection problem (arg max over |I|=r dimensions out of m′ candidates) is actually solved (greedy search, exhaustive, etc.), which is important for both reproducibility and understanding scalability to larger models or representation dimensions.

Experiments are limited to two mid-sized open models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it) and two relatively narrow unsafe-data scenarios; no evaluation at larger scale or with more diverse/heterogeneous unsafe data sources (a limitation the authors themselves acknowledge but which meaningfully limits the generality of the claims).

strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical grounding for representation-based unsafe data detection via signal detection theory, deriving a discriminability index d' that is shown empirically to be monotonically related to AUPRC (Appendix D), giving a principled objective for the proposed denoising procedure rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

The proposed DRA method (whitening + leave-target-out dimension selection) is simple, lightweight, and model-agnostic, and is shown to be broadly applicable on top of two different representation types (gradients and hidden states), consistently improving both.

Empirical gains are large and consistent across two backbones (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it) and two distinct unsafe-data scenarios (jailbreak injection and gender bias), with improvements reported not just in detection AUPRC but also in downstream retraining safety metrics (ASR, TPR Gender Gap), which strengthens the practical relevance of the detection improvements.

The gender bias experiment is a nice addition since it demonstrates the method's value in a setting where standard moderation classifiers (Wildguard, OpenAI moderation) are essentially non-functional (AUPRC ~0.05), highlighting a genuine advantage of the representation-based, taxonomy-free approach.
Ablations (Table 7) cleanly isolate the contributions of the whitening/denoising step versus the dimension-selection step, showing both matter and are complementary.

Reasonable reproducibility support: experimental details (LoRA, learning rates, epochs, hardware), evaluation protocol (Appendix A rubric, GPT-4o judge), and dataset construction (Appendix B) are described in adequate detail, and the benchmark builds on an existing standardized setup (DATE-LM).
weaknesses: The core assumption that µQ (mean of a small target set of flagged unsafe outputs) is a good proxy for µU (mean of the true unsafe training data) is central to the method but is not rigorously justified or tested beyond the target-set-size ablation in Appendix C.2; in real deployments the relationship between observed unsafe model outputs and the actual poisoned training data that caused them could be much weaker than in the controlled injection setup used here.

Both benchmark scenarios (jailbreak injection and gender bias injection) are synthetically constructed by the authors injecting a known, homogeneous unsafe subset into a benign dataset, which the authors acknowledge in the Limitations section; this raises questions about generalization to naturally occurring, heterogeneous unsafe data or to more diverse/adaptive attacks (e.g., stealthy backdoors), which are not tested.

Results depend on selecting the dimensionality hyperparameter r=30 without an ablation showing sensitivity of results to this choice, and no guidance is given on how to select r in a new setting without ground-truth labels (the LTO criterion selects indices I but the paper doesn't explain how r itself is chosen or how robust it is).

The paper claims the plug-in whitening estimator is an approximation of the optimal linear detector, but does not discuss potential instability of computing Σ_X^{-1} in high-dimensional gradient/hidden-state spaces (regularization, numerical conditioning) beyond mentioning a two-stage PCA reduction; details of how many top eigenvectors m' are used and how this choice affects results are not reported.

Comparisons to moderation classifiers (Llama-Guard, Wildguard) are somewhat apples-to-oranges since those methods do not have access to any target set / red-teaming examples, whereas DRA and other attribution baselines are given Dtarget; this asymmetry in information access is not discussed as a caveat when claiming DRA "outperforms SOTA methods."

The retraining safety improvements (Table 3, Table 6) are sometimes fairly modest for RepSim-DRA (e.g., only -2.35 and -2.15 ASR change in Table 3) despite very large detection AUPRC gains, suggesting the link between improved detection and improved downstream safety is inconsistent and method-dependent (gradient-based attribution clearly benefits more), which somewhat undercuts the generality of the retraining safety claims.

The potential-risk discussion of adversarial manipulation of influence scores is only briefly mentioned in the Limitations without any empirical robustness check, despite this being a plausible and important threat model for a detection/filtering method intended for safety-critical use.
